teaser.text: Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, makes the chips and supporting technology that turn computers into useful machines. Its business is a chain: customers choose AMD’s designs, specialist manufacturers build them, and AMD collects the difference after paying for engineering and production.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.?

paragraphs.text: The bear case uses $11,000M, then $9,500M, before recovering to $12,000M. It assumes delayed systems, weaker adoption and cash-heavy commitments. The bull case uses $23,000M, then $33,000M and $42,000M. It requires on-time production, repeat paid deployments and successful ROCm adoption.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. really make?

paragraphs.text: Stock-based pay creates another gap between accounting profit and owner economics. AMD added the expense back to operating cash because issuing shares uses no cash immediately. Deducting the US$1,638 million expense from free cash flow leaves US$3,881 million. That is an analytical allowance for the cost borne by shareholders, not a separate cash payment. It produces real free cash flow per share of US$2.37.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, compares the share price with earnings per share. A trailing P/E uses recent earnings; a forward P/E uses expected earnings. Free-cash-flow yield compares annual cash left after equipment spending with market value. A low yield means investors receive little current cash for each dollar invested, so the valuation depends on growth.

blocks.heading: Has Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. kept its promises?

paragraphs.text: AMD did complete its stated plan to retain ZT’s design expertise and sell manufacturing; the harder test is whether future growth and rewards produce enough cash and per-share value to justify their cost.

blocks.heading: How have Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s revenue and profit trended?

paragraphs.text: Operating income was US$1,990 million, compared with a US$134 million loss a year earlier. Operating margin reached 17.3%. Data Center’s segment margin was approximately 31.3%, while Client and Gaming fell to approximately 15.2%. Net income was US$2,305 million, with EPS of US$1.39. Investment gains of US$483 million helped below operating income, so they should not be treated as chip profit.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s next results?

paragraphs.text: AMD’s next reporting event is scheduled for November 3, 2026. The September checkpoint is initial delivery to manufacturing partners near the end of Q3; the stronger test is Q4 system production and customer deployment. Components leaving a factory do not prove that a usable system has reached production.

An inventory charge reduces the recorded value of products that may no longer sell as expected. A reversal restores some value when conditions improve. Through Q4 and into 2027, investors should separate customer acceptance, cash receipts and fresh licensing decisions from accounting effects.
